nameStory: The candleflame lichen gets its evocative name from its bright yellow color that resembles the warm glow of a candle's flame. It's also called lemon lichen for the same sunny yellow hue that makes it stand out against tree bark and rocks.
description: Candleflame lichen is a small, leafy lichen that forms bright yellow patches on tree bark and rocks. It's what scientists call a foliose lichen, meaning it has flat, leaf-like lobes that spread outward from a central point. The entire patch is typically just an inch or two across, but the vivid yellow color makes it surprisingly noticeable once you know what to look for.

idTips.label: Bright yellow color
idTips.description: The entire lichen glows with a distinctive sunny yellow or lemon-yellow color that catches your eye even from a distance

idTips.label: Leafy structure
idTips.description: Forms flat, overlapping lobes that feel thin and papery when gently touched, like tiny leaves pressed against the surface

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Individual patches are usually 1-2 inches across, though several may grow near each other to form larger yellow clusters

idTips.label: Smooth texture
idTips.description: The surface feels relatively smooth to the touch, not crusty or powdery like some other lichens

idTips.label: Edge appearance
idTips.description: The edges of the lobes are typically smooth and rounded, without the fringed or hairy margins of some related species

habitat: Look for candleflame lichen on the bark of deciduous trees, especially maples, oaks, and elms in parks, yards, and forest edges throughout New England. It prefers trees in somewhat open areas with good air circulation rather than deep forest shade. You'll also occasionally spot it on rocks or old wooden fences, always in spots that get some filtered sunlight.

seasonality.spring: The yellow color becomes more vibrant as humidity increases with spring rains, making this an excellent time for spotting new patches.
seasonality.summer: Remains visible but may appear slightly duller during very dry periods. Look for it in shadier spots on hot days.
seasonality.fall: Often at its most noticeable as the bright yellow contrasts beautifully with colorful autumn leaves and wet bark.
seasonality.winter: Still visible and identifiable on bare tree trunks, where the yellow color really pops against gray bark and snow.

funFact: This tiny lichen is actually two organisms living together - a fungus and an alga - and the brilliant yellow color comes from special pigments the fungus produces to protect its algae partner from too much sunlight, like a living sunscreen factory!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with fringed candleflame lichen, but the regular candleflame has smooth, rounded lobe edges while the fringed variety has distinctly hairy or fibrous edges. Memory trick: 'smooth flame, fringed frame' - the regular candleflame is smooth, while the fringed one has a fuzzy frame around its edges.
compareHints: Candleflame lichen differs from its close relative, fringed candleflame lichen, primarily in the texture of its edges - candleflame has smooth, clean lobe margins while fringed candleflame has distinctly hairy or fibrous edges that give it a more raggedy appearance. Both share the same bright yellow color, but running your finger gently along the edge will immediately tell you which species you've found.
